title: Week 27 Quiz — Capitalism, Socialism, Labor, and Reform

questions.prompt: Which distinction is most important when comparing capitalism, socialism, and mixed economies?
choices: Treat each label as one fixed system with no internal differences
Identify who owns resources, how decisions are coordinated, what incentives operate, and how risks and benefits are distributed
Assume government participation makes an economy socialist
Assume private ownership means government has no economic role
questions.explanation: The course emphasizes diverse schools and specific institutional arrangements rather than treating economic labels as single fixed models.

questions.prompt: A labor petition demands shorter hours and safer workplaces. What is the strongest historical question to ask first?
choices: Whether the petition agrees with our modern preferences
Who created it, for whom, under what conditions, and what evidence can corroborate its claims
Whether every worker shared the same view
Whether the petition is automatically true because it is primary evidence
questions.explanation: Source analysis begins with origin, audience, context, purpose, and corroboration.

questions.prompt: Which evidence would best evaluate whether a proposed wage increase improved household welfare?
choices: Nominal wages alone
Wages together with prices, hours, employment, household needs, and other relevant evidence
The employer's opinion alone
A political slogan about wages
questions.explanation: Real welfare requires contextual measures rather than a single nominal number.

questions.prompt: Why should students distinguish description, prediction, and moral judgment in economic texts?
choices: They are interchangeable
A description of how a system works does not automatically prove a prediction or establish that an outcome is morally desirable
Moral judgments are never allowed in history
Predictions are always more reliable than evidence
questions.explanation: Different kinds of claims require different evidence and reasoning.

questions.prompt: Which statement best explains why labor reform developed through multiple organizations and strategies?
choices: Workers used only strikes
Reform could involve unions, cooperatives, mutual aid, political parties, religious movements, petitions, and government regulation
Reform came only from employers
Government regulation eliminated the need for collective action
questions.explanation: The week treats labor reform as a broad historical process involving multiple forms of organization and action.

questions.prompt: A source argues that laissez-faire will produce prosperity. Which evidence would most directly test the prediction historically?
choices: A definition of laissez-faire
Comparable evidence about production, wages, prices, employment, working conditions, and distribution before and after relevant policy changes
A later political speech
The source's popularity
questions.explanation: Predictions should be tested against relevant historical outcomes and appropriate comparison.

questions.prompt: A cooperative reformer and Marxist critic both oppose aspects of industrial capitalism but propose different solutions. What should a student conclude?
choices: They must actually support identical systems
Criticism of a system does not imply agreement about the alternative; compare mechanisms, goals, institutions, and assumptions
One source must be incorrect
All socialist traditions are identical
questions.explanation: The course explicitly distinguishes diverse socialist and reform traditions.

questions.prompt: A map shows strikes concentrated near industrial cities. What can the map establish most directly?
choices: Industrialization caused every strike
There is a spatial association that can generate questions about labor organization, industry, migration, and political conditions
All workers in those cities were union members
Strikes had the same causes everywhere
questions.explanation: Maps reveal spatial patterns; causation requires additional evidence.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest method for evaluating “Economic Ideas and Worker Demands”?
choices: Compare it with independent evidence and evaluate origin, purpose, context, perspective, and limits
Accept it automatically because it is primary evidence
Reject it because it has a point of view
Use only its strongest sentence
questions.explanation: Historical reasoning requires sourcing, contextualization, and corroboration.

questions.prompt: Which response best answers the essential question: What should markets, governments, employers, workers, and communities each control?
choices: One institution should control everything
No institution should have responsibilities
A defensible answer should specify institutional roles, explain tradeoffs, use historical evidence, and acknowledge a competing interpretation
The answer is determined by whichever ideology uses the strongest label
questions.explanation: The course asks students to reason about institutional design, tradeoffs, evidence, and competing interpretations rather than memorize an ideology.

shortResponse.prompt: Using at least three specific pieces of historical evidence, answer: What should markets, governments, employers, workers, and communities each control? Compare at least two economic or reform traditions and identify one tradeoff or limitation in your proposed arrangement.

rubric.5: Defensible institutional claim; three accurate pieces of evidence; meaningful comparison of two traditions; clear tradeoff/limitation; reasoning is historically grounded.
rubric.4: Defensible claim; three relevant pieces of evidence; comparison and tradeoff mostly clear.
rubric.3: Claim with two relevant pieces of evidence and some comparison.
rubric.2: General claim with limited evidence or weak comparison.
